paragraph.text: it's a stereotype, and even if it were true it wouldn't answer anything. What happens to animals doesn't depend on the lifestyle, clothes or politics of those who defend them. Some vegans are linked to spirituality, the counterculture or the hippie movement, but that's not the whole: veganism is found in the punk movement (vegan straight edge), in political movements, in universities and in elite sport. Research shows that prejudice against vegans is real and strong, and the stereotype serves to dismiss them without discussing the argument. And if vegans have something in common, it's the rejection of violence toward animals.
L. Attacks on veganism and vegans ·
"Vegans are all hippies, living on incense and peace and love. You can't take them seriously."
Veganism is associated with a counterculture holding unrealistic ideas about society.
Ideas coming from unrealistic groups tend to be unreliable.
So vegans' conclusions about animals don't deserve to be taken seriously.

P1 has a historical origin: natural food movements and the counterculture of the 1960s and 1970s helped spread vegetarianism. But animal ethics has other roots, and veganism today is far more varied. The bigger problem lies in P2, which judges the idea by the image of those who hold it.
: it's an attack on the person (ad hominem), not on the argument.
"Are you also anti-vaccine and living on incense?"
"Veganism is a cult, a religion." (which is L7)

Imagine someone said: "I won't listen to you because you wear a colorful T-shirt." Does that make sense? The T-shirt doesn't change whether what you said is right or wrong. It's the same with vegans: how the people who defend animals dress or live doesn't change the fact that animals feel pain.

Some vegans are linked to spirituality or the counterculture, but they're only a part. There are vegans of every kind: punks, elite athletes, doctors, university professors, business owners, people on the right and on the left. What they have in common is rejecting violence toward animals. But even if they were all hippies, what would that change for the pig? He would still feel pain just the same. You may not like the speaker's style, and the argument still stands. The question is about the pig, not about anyone's clothes: is it right to put him through that?
"If the same idea were said by someone in a suit, would it become more correct?"
The argument swaps the question about the idea for a question about who holds it:
Is it just to cause that suffering for a taste?
Judging an idea by the image of those who hold it is a classic error. An animal's pain doesn't depend on anyone's haircut.

Some vegans are indeed linked to spirituality, natural food, the counterculture or the hippie movement. But that's only a part. Vegans are found in every profession, income bracket and political position, and the image of the "hippie" describes, at most, a part of a part.

text.bold: 3. Veganism is found in very different places.

paragraph.text: Since the late 1980s, part of the straight edge hardcore scene (which rejects alcohol and drugs) took up vegetarianism and later veganism. In the 1990s, bands such as Earth Crisis put animal rights at the center of their lyrics, and "vegan straight edge" emerged. A more radical, minority strand, hardline, arose in the same scene and was rejected by much of it.

There are political parties and movements focused on animals, such as the Party for the Animals, which has held seats in the Dutch parliament since 2006, and animal advocates across very different political currents.
Animal ethics is discussed in philosophy, law and science departments by authors from different schools (point 5).

Racing driver Lewis Hamilton announced in 2017 that he had gone vegan and then won four more Formula 1 world titles. Strength athlete Patrik Baboumian, a vegan, set the Guinness record in 2013 for the heaviest yoke carried over 10 meters (555.2 kg).

Research shows that vegans and vegetarians are the target of negative attitudes equal to or greater than those directed at several other groups. The hippie label is one way of expressing that prejudice: instead of answering the argument, it ridicules whoever makes it.
The central argument of veganism comes from moral philosophy, discussed in universities by authors from different schools, not from a countercultural aesthetic.

text.bold: 6. What vegans have in common is the rejection of violence toward animals.

paragraph.text: No studies show that vegans are, as people, more peaceful than others. But veganism is, by definition, a refusal to take part in violence toward animals, as far as is possible and practicable. That's what vegan punks, athletes, professors and hippies share, and it's what the argument fails to discuss.
That a group has wrong ideas on some subjects doesn't show it's wrong on all of them. Each claim has to be assessed on what it says.
Omnivores evaluated vegetarians and vegans equally or more negatively than several common prejudice target groups; vegans were evaluated more negatively than vegetarians
Meat eaters tend to disparage vegetarians because they expect to be judged by them

It's right that veganism has historical roots intersecting with the counterculture, that some vegans are linked to spirituality or the hippie movement, and that a movement's public image affects how its ideas are received. Thinking about communication is legitimate.
But the image of those who hold an idea doesn't decide whether it's true. Animals feel pain whoever says so.
